hook: Rocks in China dated at 3.95 billion years sank 50 kilometers deep.

sections.voiceover: Rocks in China dated at 3.95 billion years sank 50 kilometers deep.
sections.visual_cue: Macro shot of ancient crystalline rock formation with glowing depth graphics showing 50 kilometer depth marker.
sections.sfx_cue: Deep sub-bass rumble with low seismic thud
b_roll: Geological rock strata close up shot

sections.voiceover: In Hebei Province, Yusheng Wan identified ancient crust in the Shimen Complex. Earth formed 4.5 billion years ago, leaving few ancient rocks. Where did this 3.95 billion year old crust go?
sections.visual_cue: Satellite view highlighting Hebei Province transitioning to geological map of the Shimen Complex.
sections.sfx_cue: Gentle ambient synth wave followed by subtle chime
b_roll: Satellite map zoom into Hebei Province China
Geologists inspecting rock samples in field

sections.voiceover: But Nature reported the crust rapidly plunged over 50 kilometers deep and partially melted.
sections.visual_cue: 3D Earth mantel diagram showing oceanic crust plunging rapidly into subterranean heat layers.
b_roll: Scientific journal page graphic for Nature

sections.voiceover: They've found 3.95 billion year old oceanic crust in the Jidong region that partially melted. They are Asia's oldest rocks, behind Canada's 4.0 billion year old Acasta Gneiss.
sections.visual_cue: Comparative timeline showing Jidong rocks alongside Canada Acasta Gneiss with thermal magma graphics.

sections.voiceover: Ancient crust sank 50 kilometers in Earth's early history.
sections.visual_cue: Cinematic wide shot of rocky geological outcrop under golden hour light.
b_roll: Panoramic view of rugged mountains in northern China
